summary: Registers ENUM services for Internet calendaring. It covers scheduling with iMIP, the iCalendar message-based interoperability protocol, and accessing calendar information with CalDAV. These let a telephone number or other identifier be linked to calendar services. It is on the standards track and was later updated by RFC 6118.

plainLanguage.summary: A phone number can point to someone's calendar too. This registers the labels that tell a lookup system whether a calendar can take invitations or can be browsed.

subtitle: Registers the ENUM labels that let a phone number point to a person's calendar for invitations or for browsing.

tldr.problem: ENUM turns telephone numbers into URIs, but there was no registered label saying that a URI leads to a calendar for scheduling or for access to calendar data.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC registers two Enumservices: ical-sched with subtype mailto for iMIP scheduling by email, and ical-access with subtypes http and https for CalDAV access.
tldr.outcome: A DNS record for a phone number can now advertise a scheduling address and a calendar-access address. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and was later updated by RFC 6118.

today: RFC 5333 is a Proposed Standard that was later updated by RFC 6118. Read the two together for the current registrations.

sections.title: Why Calendar Enumservices
sections.content:
ENUM (E.164 Number Mapping, RFC 3761) uses the Domain Name System to translate a telephone number such as +12025550100 into a URI such as mailto:user@example.com. It exists mainly to connect systems that use telephone numbers with those that use URIs.

The RFC gives a concrete use: a phone could check the free/busy status of someone in its address book, or propose a meeting with them, starting from the person's phone number. This document registers the Enumservices needed to make that possible for Internet calendaring.
sections.plainLanguage: You know someone's phone number. This RFC lets your phone use that number to find their calendar, a bit like looking up an address from a name.

sections.title: The Calendaring Protocols Involved
sections.content:
The RFC quotes the Guide to Internet Calendaring (RFC 3283) to place the pieces. iCalendar is the language used to describe calendar objects. iTIP describes how to use iCalendar to do scheduling. iMIP describes how to do iTIP scheduling via e-mail.

A newer Standards Track protocol, CalDAV (RFC 4791), is based on WebDAV. It manipulates Internet calendars and views free/busy lists, and a planned scheduling extension could later be used to propose events too.

These services are already addressed by existing URI schemes: mailto: for iMIP-compatible calendar services, and http: and https: for CalDAV-compatible ones.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two ways to deal with a calendar. One is to email an invitation, and the other is to open the calendar over the web. Each already has its own kind of address.

sections.title: The Registered Enumservices
sections.content:
Following the templates of RFC 3761, the RFC registers two Enumservice names. Both are marked with intended usage COMMON, and the author is given as Rohan Mahy.

  • ical-sched with subtype mailto and URI scheme mailto:. The URI can be used for scheduling with Internet calendaring via Internet mail, using iMIP.
  • ical-access with subtype http and URI scheme http:. The URI can be used to access a user's calendar, for example free/busy status, using CalDAV.
  • ical-access with subtype https and URI scheme https:, with the same purpose as the http subtype.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two tags. One says send invitations here by email. The other says look at the calendar here on the web.

sections.title: The Dash in the Type Names
sections.content:
Both types contain a dash, as in ical-sched. The RFC explains that the Enumservices need hierarchical concepts, so some kind of boundary has to separate the parts of the name. Neither RFC 3761 nor its intended successor foresees sub-subtyping.

Using a dash is therefore described as slightly contradictory to RFC 3761. The intended successors clearly allow a dash in Type strings, so the authors treat it as a practical way forward.
sections.plainLanguage: The tag names have a small dash in the middle to split them into parts. The old rules did not plan for that, but the newer rules do, so the authors went ahead.

sections.title: Example DNS Records
sections.content: The RFC shows two NAPTR records under the same E.164 name. The first, with the service field E2U+ical-access:https, maps to an HTTPS calendar URL. The second, with E2U+ical-sched:mailto, maps to a mailto: address. The numbers 10 and 20 are the order values of the two records.
sections.plainLanguage: The phone number's listing has two lines. One line says where to browse the calendar, and the other says where to email invitations.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
DNS makes no policy decisions about which records it gives out, so all records must be assumed available to all inquirers at all times. ENUM data is therefore open to the public. A calendaring URI alone is unlikely to cause many privacy problems, although depending on its structure it might reveal the full name or employer of the target. Anonymous URIs mitigate this.

DNS in its current form offers no way to confirm that an answer is authentic. Many of these problems are prevented when the resolver verifies answers with DNSSEC, where it is available. Threat analyses are in RFC 3761 and RFC 3833.

The more serious concern is attack on the calendaring system itself, such as unauthorized modification or viewing. iTIP lists security requirements for authentication, integrity and confidentiality, and CalDAV over https: uses TLS for server authentication, confidentiality and message integrity. Calendar URIs are often already guessable and usually need credentials, so revealing an unprotected calendar through ENUM is unlikely in practice.
sections.plainLanguage: A phone number listing is like a public phone book, so anyone can see it. The real protection is that the calendar itself asks for a password before showing anything.
